title: Two Big Things My Mom Taught Me About Savoring Life
author: Arthur Brooks
source: How to Build a Life Newsletter (arthurbrooks.com)
summary: Arthur Brooks reflects on his late mother—a Pacific Northwest watercolor artist—and her simple but profound advice about learning to draw: actually look at what you're drawing, because the mind fills in perceived details with assumptions rather than observation. Brooks uses this lesson as a framework for savoring, the psychological practice of attending fully to positive experiences across past, present, and future dimensions of time. A 2012 daily diary study (Jose, Lim & Bryant) found that subjects asked to savor pleasant events were significantly happier after the experiment than control counterparts; follow-up research (Colombo et al., 2024) shows that savoring experiences more vividly at the time also makes them more fondly recalled later. Brooks offers two practical rules: distribute savoring across all three temporal dimensions and identify which is personally weakest to develop; and build a daily savoring practice using morning anticipation, present-moment awareness, and evening gratitude expressed to someone involved. The underlying insight is that happiness depends not on the volume of positive experiences but on the quality of attention brought to them—a faculty that can be deliberately trained and becomes more valuable as time grows shorter.
points: 'Actually looking' at what you draw—rather than relying on mental shorthand—is a direct analogy for savoring: most people glance at positive experiences and let the brain fill in assumptions, missing the full encounter with what's actually in front of them.

Research shows that savoring positive experiences more fully at the time makes them more vividly and fondly recallable later—the happiness benefit is not just immediate but stored as a memory asset that compounds over time.

Savoring has three temporal dimensions—past reminiscence, present enjoyment, and future anticipation—and people benefit most from identifying and strengthening whichever dimension is weakest in their own disposition.

Brooks's personal daily savoring protocol: morning anticipation (two or three vivid previews with intentional smiling), present-moment awareness during the events themselves, and evening gratitude expressed aloud to at least one person involved in the day's best moments.

Savoring becomes increasingly important as we age because it allows us to extract richer value from a shorter remaining horizon of experience—less time ahead is not a curse if the savoring faculty is actively cultivated.
quotes: 'People almost never actually look carefully at anything; they glance at it and then rely on their brain to fill in the details—which it doesn't, leading to a crummy drawing.'
This kind of savoring, it turns out, can help us become more adept at living and make us much happier.
Savoring positive experiences leads to happier memories later on. Research shows that people who savor good times can recall them more vividly, and therefore look back on them more fondly.
These findings are important, especially as we age. Having less time on Earth doesn't have to be a curse if we savor our experiences well.

I start my morning with a quick reflection on two or three things I'm looking forward to... I imagined each of these events vividly for a few seconds, and made an effort to smile as I did so. Then, when the events themselves occur, I try to be fully present and conscious of the fact that I'm doing something I like.
